extracted.intended_audience: children and elementary-level readers (and their teachers/parents)
extracted.subtask_description: A short, illustrated natural-history chapter explaining anatomy, life-cycles, behaviors, and classification of grasshoppers, katydids, crickets, and related insects for young readers. Emphasizes observable characters and simple comparative taxonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leg orientation and function (front/middle/hind)
rubrics_metrics.description: The front pair are directed forward. The middle and hind legs are directed backward. When the insect walks, the front legs pull and the middle and hind legs push.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use leg direction and role (pulling vs pushing) to describe locomotion; observe which legs touch the ground and how they move during walking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modified appendages indicate special function
rubrics_metrics.description: When any part is changed from the regular shape or size, we say it is modified. The front legs of the mantis are modified to catch and hold its prey. The hind legs of the grasshopper are modified to jump with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for enlarged or altered segments (e.g., enlarged trochanter, femur, spiny tibia) to infer specialized uses such as grasping, digging, or jumping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mantis grasping-leg morphology
rubrics_metrics.description: Mantis front legs: coxa small and close to body; trochanter very large and long; femur large and strong with a row of sharp spiny teeth; tibia also supplied with teeth; joint between tibia and femur is a strong hinge allowing tibia to shut close to femur forming a trap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify predatory (grasping) habits by these specific segment enlargements and spines; note hinge joint allowing locking of tibia and femur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grasshopper hind-leg adaptation for jumping
rubrics_metrics.description: Hind legs are modified to jump with; segments change in shape and size compared with regular legs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess jumping ability by looking for enlarged hind femur/tibia and overall limb proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wing cover (roof wings) vs inner flying wings
rubrics_metrics.description: The roof wings (wing covers) lie along each side of the body and come together on top like the ridge of a sloping house roof; folded under them is a pair of delicate gauzy inner wings which are used for flying. The locust does not fly with the wing covers; it flies with the inner wings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identifying flying vs protective structures, look for hard/stiff wing covers versus delicate inner wings; observe how they fold and overlap when at rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wing folding and spring action
rubrics_metrics.description: The inner wings fold under the wing covers like little fans; the wing joints act like springs so the wings close of themselves. Wing covers can lock open and stay open without effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe wing mechanics: whether wings self-close, whether covers lock open—these behaviors explain how insects manage flying vs resting postures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colourful inner wings used only during flight
rubrics_metrics.description: Some grasshoppers have brightly colored inner (flying) wings—yellow or red—and show their gay inner wings only during flight; as soon as they rest the inner wings close and are hidden by the wing covers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sudden flashes of color in flight as an identifying behavior; note that color may be hidden when insect is at rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wing development and moulting (larval wing pads)
rubrics_metrics.description: When first hatched the locust larva is like the full-grown locust but very small and with no wings. As it grows it moults; the wings begin to show as little pads at its sides and are moulted off with the next skin until the grasshopper is full-grown with full-sized wings. The wings of the insect are only modified parts of the skin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize incomplete metamorphosis by presence of wing pads and sequential moults; wingless juveniles that gradually acquire wings through moulting indicate Orthoptera-like development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egg-laying behavior and ovipositor function
rubrics_metrics.description: Some lay eggs in holes in the ground made by the strong, sharp end of the abdomen; eggs are covered with a sticky substance to keep out wet. Female katydids and some grasshoppers have a long sword-shaped ovipositor used to roughen bark or make holes and guide eggs to be fastened with a gummy substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify egg-laying strategy (ground vs twigs) by presence and shape of ovipositor; observe whether eggs overwinter in ground and are glued/covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abdomen segmentation and chitinous exoskeleton
rubrics_metrics.description: The abdomen shows ten rings (segments), each ring covered with a hard horny substance called chitin. Each ring is made of four pieces (back, two sides, under) so the insect can move; segments are fastened by soft skin allowing telescoping lengthening/shortening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use segment counts (ten rings) and presence of chitinous plates to distinguish insect body plan and to explain mobility mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoracic segmentation and appendage attachment
rubrics_metrics.description: The thorax has three segments grown close together: front segment bears the front legs; middle segment bears the middle pair of legs and the wing covers; hind segment bears the long hind legs and the flying wings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine which appendages attach to which thoracic segment to classify function (walking, wing-bearing, jumping).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exoskeletal musculature and strength-to-size comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Insects have muscles inside their chitinous shells; muscles are very strong—stronger for their size than a horse's muscles. Many insects can pull loads several times their body weight (example: bee can pull twenty times its weight).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use relative muscle-power observations (ability to pull/jump) as functional evidence when describing insect capabilities; not a taxonomic character but useful for behavioral description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing organs placement and mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Some grasshoppers have a little flat membrane (eardrum) on the tibia of each front leg; other species have sensitive spots on antennæ or even on the abdomen. The eardrum vibrates and excites the nerve of hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize ears by looking for membranes on tibia or sensitive spots on antennae/abdomen; hearing structure location varies across species but serves the same vibratory function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound production (stridulation) mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Males often have modified parts for producing sound: many grasshoppers rub upper end of inner wings against wing covers, or male wing covers are ribbed/divided into spaces like drum-heads and a ridge that acts like a file. Rubbing produces chirping/stridulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify males by musical structures (scraper, file, vibrating membranes) on wing covers or wings; observe rubbing behavior to confirm stridulation mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing longhorned (meadow) vs shorthorned (locust) grasshoppers
rubrics_metrics.description: Longhorned (meadow) grasshoppers have long, thread-like antennæ longer than the body and tarsus with four joints instead of three; they are generally more slender and delicate in shape and some males have ears on their front legs. Shorthorned (locusts) differ in antennæ length and ovipositor shape/egg-laying behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use antennal length, number of tarsal joints, body build, and presence/location of ears to separate longhorned vs shorthorned groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cricket identification by wing cover structure and song
rubrics_metrics.description: Crickets have flat-backed wing covers (not peaked), often overlapping; male wing covers are heavily ribbed and divided into spaces like little drum-heads; he raises and rubs wing covers together to chirp. Females lack ovipositor and have different wing ornamentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate crickets from grasshoppers by body shape (flat back), wing cover ribbing, and male stridulatory behavior; observe seasonal timing (chirping seen in fall when wings are fully grown).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized morphologies within crickets (mole cricket, tree cricket)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mole crickets burrow and have fore legs modified into strong digging tools resembling paws; tree crickets are pale green and may be mistaken for other small insects but have cricket form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for foreleg modification to identify burrowing species and coloration/habitat (trees, rocks, hearth) for other cricket types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping Orthoptera by lifestyle and morphology
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested mnemonic grouping: Running Orthoptera (cockroaches); Grasping Orthoptera (praying mantis); Walking Orthoptera (walking sticks); Jumping/Jumping Orthoptera (shorthorned grasshoppers/locusts, longhorned grasshoppers, crickets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group insects into functional categories based on locomotion and appendage specialization to aid memory and identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Orthoptera diagnostic features
rubrics_metrics.description: Orthoptera: four wings (upper narrow/stiff as wing covers, inner broader and delicate and fold up), mouth parts made to bite (chewing, not sucking), young look like adults but without wings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use wing type, mouthpart function, and life-cycle (incomplete metamorphosis) as primary diagnostic characters for Orthoptera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative diagnostic features for other insect orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Odonata (dragonflies): four wings all alike, stiff and covered with a close network of fine veins, no wing covers. Ephemerida (mayflies): hind wings much smaller. Plecoptera (stoneflies): hind wings folded in plaits. Thysanura (silverfish): no wings, bristled tail. Hemiptera (true bugs): mouth parts form a tube for piercing and sucking; young are like adults (no dramatic metamorphosis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying an insect beyond Orthoptera, compare wing venation and folding, hind-wing proportions, presence/absence of wing covers, mouthpart type (chewing vs piercing-sucking), and juvenile-adult similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hemiptera (true bugs) diagnostic notes
rubrics_metrics.description: A bug has four wings (when present) but wings differ from Orthoptera; bugs commonly have mouth parts grown together into a tube used to pierce and suck, and their young are like the adults (only smaller and wingless).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify an insect as Hemiptera if it uses a beak-like tube to pierce and suck and if juvenile forms resemble adults; observe feeding mode (sucking vs biting/chewing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Field observation advice for learning insects
rubrics_metrics.description: The best way is to use your own eyes and watch. Lie down perfectly still in the grass and soon the insects will appear; listen to their sounds to learn to know different insects by their calls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ patient, direct observation and listening to learn identification and behavior; sound can be diagnostic for species or groups.
